extracted.intended_audience: American statesmen, framers, and citizens interested in constitutional design (late-18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for designing stable republican constitutions and governmental institutions that preserve liberty, prevent faction, and secure property through separation of powers and balanced orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three orders and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments must be supported and enforced by three different orders of men in equilibrio; without three orders and a balance, caprice, instability, turbulence, revolutions, tyranny and anarchy follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams asserts repeatedly that the protection of laws and liberty depends on equal laws 'made by common consent, and supported, protected, and enforced by three different orders of men in equilibrio.' The history of Italian republics is used as evidence that the absence of a balanced three-order structure leads to frequent revolutions and degeneration into tyranny or anarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government (division of authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed constitution — combining elements or separate orders (one, few, many) and/or a supreme executive head or senate — is generally preferable to a simple single-assembly government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams argues that pure democracies or pure aristocracies tend to divide into factions; 'a popular government was never so free or so durable as when it was mixed with the authority of one supreme head, or of a senate.' He critiques simple single-assembly governments which 'must of necessity divide into two parties.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of judicial power
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial authority should be separated from legislative/executive functions and be independent enough that people can trust judges to decide impartially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Florence the people distrusted the anziani with judicial power so they appointed foreign judges — illustrating the need for separated, impartial judiciary. Adams emphasizes that judicial power must be distinct and protected from transient popular passions and factions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and negatives among branches/estates
rubrics_metrics.description: Different branches or estates should possess negatives or vetoes over each other to prevent any single faction or assembly from gaining unchecked power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Neuchatel where 'the legislative authority resides conjunctively in the prince, the council of state, and the town or people, each of which has a negative.' Adams endorses multi-branch arrangements because 'two branches, with each a negative' help reconcile law and liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct and preserved orders (avoid mixing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mix aristocratic and democratic elements indiscriminately in the same bodies; keep orders separate so their opposing interests can check each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams criticizes Florence's 'jumble' where buonhomini, credenza, and other assemblies were 'all huddled together in the general council' — leading inevitably to factional dominance by the nobility. He identifies mixing of orders as a fatal defect producing never-ending factions and civil war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and protection of the middle (propertied) class
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantial middle order of citizens (those of property and moderate wealth) is essential and 'extremely useful' in proportioning and stabilizing a perfect republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams notes that the middling citizens (the 'people of property') act as a corrective to extremes of nobles and plebeians; good constitutions should preserve and empower this class to prevent perpetual revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term limits, rotation, and tenure appropriate to stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistracies and offices should have clear rules on tenure — short annual terms can be ineffective, while holding offices 'during good behaviour' may better secure impartial administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams describes Florentine annual magistracies as insufficient ('the twelve anziani... annually eligible — a form of government... ineffectual') and contrasts with Neuchatel where magistrates 'hold their employments during good behaviour,' suggesting thoughtful design of term lengths to balance accountability and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded powers and clear allocation of magistracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions should clearly delineate 'the bounds of rules and magistracy' — who ought to govern and who must obey — so as to prevent uncertainty about sovereignty and instability of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams laments ancient constitutions' 'incertitude of the sovereignty' and recommends fixed, explicit divisions of legislative, executive, and judicial responsibilities to avoid contests decided by the sword.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms to prevent and mitigate faction
rubrics_metrics.description: Because political communities naturally divide into competing passions and factions, constitutions must include institutions (multiple orders, checks, separation) that expose and remedy causes of discord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams uses many Italian examples to show factions lead to executions, confiscations, banishments, assassinations. He recommends learning from historical causes of discord and establishing balances that 'reconcile law and liberty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial due process and local trial safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens should not be tried outside the country or otherwise than by the proper judges; personal liberty must be tenderly and securely protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Neuchatel 'No citizen can be tried out of the country, or otherwise than by the judges.' Adams uses such protections as exemplars of sound constitutional safeguards for personal liberty and property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers bound by oaths to maintain rights and customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereigns and executives should be formally bound (e.g., by oath) to maintain the rights, liberties, franchises, and customs (written or unwritten) of their people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams notes the king of Neuchatel 'at his accession, takes an oath to maintain all the rights, liberties, franchises, and customs,' as a constitutional check and moral commitment that constrains executive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular convocation and accountability of representative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative assemblies and estates should be regularly convened (e.g., annually) and have defined roles and confirmatory powers to ensure continuity and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neuchatel's 'three estates... shall be assembled every year' and act as the superior tribunal; Adams recommends regular meetings and institutionalized procedures to avoid ad hoc power grabs and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilian control and organization of the militia
rubrics_metrics.description: Military forces (militias) should be organized under civil magistracy and subordinate to civic authorities to avoid military usurpation of political power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Florence 'railed twenty bands or companies in the city' with youth obliged to be ready-armed under the captain of the anziani — an example showing militia under civic command; Adams implies military organization must be accountable to civil institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial selection of judges and use of outsiders to secure fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where local bias is expected, appointing non-local or carefully chosen impartial judges can preserve trust in administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Florence appointed two judges who were not Florentines 'to prevent any feuds or discontents' in judiciary matters; Adams presents this as a practical measure to secure impartial adjudication where factional local influence is strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on sovereign's direct interference in judicial discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives should not be sole judges of the behaviour of magistrates; disciplinary procedures should be vested in other institutions or judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams observes 'magistrates and officers of justice hold their employments during good behaviour; nor is the king the judge of ill behaviour' in Neuchatel, recommending institutional safeguards against executive caprice in judging officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic openness and encouragement of settlement and commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that encourage strangers to settle and grant liberal trade privileges strengthen population, commerce, and the state's prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams praises Neuchatel's 'liberal encouragement' to strangers and privileges of trade as contributing to population growth and prosperity, contrasting with narrower Swiss cantons where restrictive policy depressed population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of honors and appointment power in a single unified assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive power to dispose public honours and offices should not be vested in a single joint assembly that mixes all orders, as that enables one class to dominate through election influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adams criticizes Florence for giving 'the executive power, the power of disposing public honours and offices, to a joint assemblage of buonhomini, credenza, and the two other assemblies, all in one' which permits the nobility to capture power — an anti-pattern to avoid.
